promptText: Why is Base62 encoding of a unique numeric ID preferred over hashing (e.g. truncated MD5) for generating short URL codes?
options: Base62 is a deterministic encoding of an already-unique number, so it guarantees zero collisions by construction, unlike hashing which can collide and forces a retry or uniqueness check on every insert
Base62 produces longer codes that are easier for users to remember than a hash
Hashing cannot be computed quickly enough for a high-traffic URL shortener
Base62 encoding automatically expires old short URLs after a fixed retention period
explanation: Because Base62 simply re-encodes a number that is already guaranteed unique (an auto-increment or Snowflake-style ID), the resulting code cannot collide, whereas hashing can produce the same output for different inputs and requires extra collision handling on every write.

promptText: Why should large files like resumes be stored in object storage (e.g. S3) rather than as database BLOBs?
options: BLOBs bloat the database, slow backups and restores, and compete with transactional queries for I/O and buffer-pool resources that object storage isolates entirely
Relational databases are physically incapable of storing binary data of any size
Object storage provides ACID transaction guarantees that a relational database cannot
Storing files in a database prevents the application from ever generating a downloadable URL for them
explanation: Large binary files stored as BLOBs cause uncontrolled database growth, make backups and restores slower and costlier, and can evict useful query data from the buffer pool during large-file reads, whereas object storage is purpose-built for large, durable, cheaply replicated content and leaves the database holding only lightweight metadata and a reference URL.

promptText: Why is Token Bucket the most common production choice among rate-limiting algorithms?
options: It balances a steady average rate with tolerance for short bursts, which matches real, bursty user behavior better than a strictly uniform output rate
It is the only algorithm that can be implemented without any shared state across servers
It guarantees zero requests are ever throttled, unlike the other algorithms
It requires no configuration of a refill rate or bucket capacity, unlike sliding window
explanation: Token Bucket refills tokens at a fixed rate up to a capacity, so it enforces a steady long-run rate while still allowing a client to burst up to the bucket's capacity, which matches real traffic patterns better than Fixed Window's boundary-burst problem or Leaky Bucket's strictly smooth output.

promptText: Why must a client-retried POST request (such as "apply to job") be protected with an idempotency key, while a retried PUT or DELETE does not need one?
options: POST typically creates a new resource on every call, so retrying it can create duplicates, whereas PUT replaces a resource to the same end state and DELETE leaves it deleted regardless of how many times it is repeated
PUT and DELETE are processed asynchronously, so retries are automatically deduplicated by the server
POST requests cannot carry a request body, making deduplication impossible
Idempotency keys are only relevant for GET requests, not for any write operation
explanation: An idempotent method produces the same end state no matter how many times it runs; PUT and DELETE satisfy this naturally, but POST usually creates a new record each call, so a retried POST (from a timeout or network blip) needs an explicit idempotency key to avoid creating duplicate resources like double applications.

promptText: What is the expected impact on the system if Redis goes down, assuming it is used purely as a cache?
options: Performance degrades because the database becomes the fallback source for what the cache used to serve, but the system should continue functioning
The entire system becomes completely unavailable, identical to a database outage
All previously cached data is permanently and irrecoverably lost from the source of truth
Write operations across the whole system stop working entirely
explanation: Redis is a cache, not the source of truth, so its failure should degrade performance (higher latency, more database load) rather than cause an outage; the real risk to manage is a stampede of full traffic suddenly hitting the database, which is why a replicated Redis cluster and load shedding are recommended mitigations.

promptText: Why is a composite unique constraint on (user_id, job_id) the correct way to prevent duplicate job applications, rather than an application-level "check then insert"?
options: A check-then-insert in application code is unsafe under concurrency, since two racing requests can both read "no existing application" and both insert; the database constraint rejects the second insert atomically regardless of timing
Application-level checks are slower than database constraints but otherwise equally correct
Unique constraints are the only way to add an index to a table in PostgreSQL
The unique constraint automatically retries a failed insert until it succeeds
explanation: Two concurrent requests can both pass an application-level existence check before either has inserted, letting both duplicates through; a database-level unique constraint closes that race because the database itself rejects the second conflicting insert no matter how the requests interleave.

promptText: What is the key durability risk of the write-behind (write-back) caching pattern compared to write-through?
options: If the cache fails before flushing its buffered writes to the database, those recent writes are lost and the database is left inconsistent with what the cache had accepted
Write-behind requires every read to also hit the database, eliminating any caching benefit
Write-behind cannot be combined with a TTL, so cached data never expires
Write-behind always produces higher write latency than write-through because it double-writes synchronously
explanation: Write-behind returns success to the application after writing only to the cache, persisting to the database asynchronously and often in batches; if the cache crashes before that flush happens, those writes are permanently lost, making it the most operationally risky of the three caching patterns despite its low write latency.

promptText: A popular cache key expires and hundreds of concurrent requests immediately miss and hit the database at once. Which combination of techniques directly addresses this cache stampede?
options: A distributed lock so only one request rebuilds the expired key while others wait or serve stale data, combined with randomized TTL jitter so many keys do not expire at the same instant
Switching the eviction policy from LRU to random eviction
Increasing the database's connection pool size so it can absorb the full concurrent load
Disabling the cache entirely for that specific key going forward
explanation: A distributed lock ensures the database sees a single recomputation instead of a flood of simultaneous misses, while jittered TTLs prevent many hot keys from expiring in the same instant in the first place; cache warming is the third standard technique, pre-populating hot keys before they are needed.

promptText: A system adds read replicas to scale reads. A user updates their profile and, immediately after, reads it back and sees the old value. What is the most likely cause, and what is the standard fix?
options: Replication lag between the primary and the replica; reads that need the absolute latest data (read-your-writes) should be routed to the primary instead of a replica
The database's unique constraint was violated during the update, silently discarding it
The CDN cached the old profile page and needs to be purged
The application server that handled the write crashed before committing the transaction
explanation: Read replicas are asynchronously and eventually consistent with the primary, so a read immediately following a write can land on a replica that has not yet applied it; the standard design routes read-your-writes-sensitive queries to the primary and accepts eventual consistency for the rest.

promptText: What is the most common root cause of a "hot partition" in a sharded database, and what is a direct mitigation?
options: A low-cardinality or naturally skewed shard key concentrates traffic on one shard; mitigations include a higher-cardinality or composite shard key, or hashing/salting to spread the hot key across shards
Hot partitions only occur when replication factor is set below 3
Hot partitions are caused exclusively by running too few read replicas, unrelated to the shard key
The only fix for a hot partition is to immediately re-shard the entire dataset onto a completely different database engine
explanation: A shard key that does not distribute data or traffic evenly (or a naturally skewed access pattern, like one viral entity) concentrates load on a single shard, defeating the purpose of sharding; choosing a higher-cardinality key, adding salting, or caching the hot entity in front of the database are the standard mitigations rather than a wholesale re-shard.

promptText: Why do interviewers push back on sticky sessions and steer candidates toward stateless services?
options: Sticky sessions cause uneven traffic distribution and lose a user's session if their pinned server dies, and they block clean horizontal scaling since new instances cannot inherit existing sessions
Sticky sessions are incompatible with the round-robin load-balancing algorithm and cannot be configured alongside it
Sticky sessions require every server to run the exact same operating system version
Sticky sessions prevent a load balancer from performing health checks on backend instances
explanation: Pinning a user to one server undermines even load distribution and makes that user's session unrecoverable if the server fails, and it prevents new instances from serving existing users; externalizing session state (Redis or a client-held JWT) keeps services stateless so any instance can serve any request and the load balancer can freely use round robin or least connections.

promptText: Why does a job portal push search index updates through Kafka events rather than writing to the search index synchronously in the same request that creates a job?
options: It decouples the write path from the search cluster's availability and performance, so a slow or down search index causes a harmless backlog of events instead of failing user writes
Kafka is required because Elasticsearch/OpenSearch cannot accept direct write requests from any application
Synchronous indexing would violate the job portal's database's unique constraint on applications
Event-driven indexing eliminates the eventual consistency between the database and the search index entirely
explanation: Publishing an event and letting a consumer update the search index asynchronously means the write path is never blocked by or coupled to the search cluster's health; the accepted cost is a short eventual-consistency window before a new job appears in search, which is standard for discovery use cases.

promptText: Comparing a Kafka outage to a database outage in a job portal built with async notifications and event-driven search indexing, why does one qualify as a critical outage and the other does not?
options: The database holds the source of truth so its loss breaks writes and most reads outright, while Kafka backs only asynchronous pipelines (notifications, search indexing), so its failure delays those features while core synchronous APIs like login, posting, and applying should keep working
Both outages are equally critical because Kafka also stores the authoritative copy of every job and application record
A Kafka outage is strictly worse because it immediately blocks all database writes across every service
Neither outage matters in practice because both systems are always deployed as a single node with no replication
explanation: Because Kafka only carries asynchronous, decoupled work, its outage is contained to delaying notifications and search updates while the synchronous core APIs continue to function; the database is different because it is the authoritative source of truth for every core operation, so its outage is the one classified as a true critical outage requiring replication, failover, and a disaster-recovery plan with defined RPO/RTO.

promptText: A system suddenly receives 10x traffic. Following the senior-level scaling framework described for this scenario, what is the correct order of levers to apply, and why?
options: Scale out stateless application instances, add a CDN for static content, and lean on Redis and read replicas first, since these are cheap and high-leverage; only reach for sharding or CQRS on the data tier once those simpler measures are exhausted
Immediately shard the primary database by user_id before touching the application or cache tier, since sharding is the fastest lever to deploy under pressure
Introduce sticky sessions across all application instances first to guarantee consistent routing during the traffic spike
Disable the CDN and route all static content through the origin servers to simplify the architecture during the spike
explanation: Because the application tier is stateless, horizontal scaling behind the load balancer is the first and cheapest lever, paired with a CDN for static content and Redis/read replicas to shield the database; sharding and CQRS introduce real complexity (shard-key selection, cross-shard queries, rebalancing) and are reserved for when write volume genuinely exceeds what caching and replicas can absorb.

promptText: A rate limiter is implemented with the Token Bucket algorithm, but each of ten application instances keeps its own in-memory token count for a given client. Why is this broken, and what does the correct fix rely on?
options: A client could effectively get up to ten times the intended limit since each instance enforces the limit independently; the fix requires a shared store like Redis with atomic operations (INCR/Lua scripting) so all instances see and update one consistent token count
The bug is unrelated to distribution and is actually caused by using Token Bucket instead of Fixed Window
In-memory counters are fine as long as the load balancer uses round robin instead of least connections
The fix is to increase each instance's bucket capacity by a factor of ten to compensate for the duplication
explanation: If the limit is enforced per-instance rather than globally, a client hitting different instances can accumulate up to N times the intended quota across N instances; the limit must be enforced against one shared, atomically-updated counter, which is exactly why Redis (fast, atomic INCR/EXPIRE, usable by every instance) is the standard backing store for distributed rate limiting.
